definition: An editorial is classified as about 'Americanism and Guns' when it explicitly and substantively connects firearms, gun ownership, shooting, or gun rights to American national identity, founding heritage, constitutional rights (especially the Second Amendment and the right to keep and bear arms), liberty and freedom, civic virtue, or the citizen-soldier/'prepared citizenry' ideal of national defense; or when it frames gun control as a foreign, un-American, or tyrannical practice (e.g., European, Soviet/Communist, Fascist, Gestapo, or police-state measures).
clarification: Include as 1 any editorial that does one or more of the following as a substantive or recurring theme: (a) defends gun ownership, the gun industry, or shooters by invoking the Constitution, the Bill of Rights, the Second Amendment, the right to keep and bear arms, or 'freedom' and 'liberty'; (b) ties firearms to the Founders, the Revolution, the frontier/West, or claims that armed citizens won, built, or defend America (e.g., Minute Men, Davy Crockett, 'a nation of marksmen/riflemen'); (c) presents a marksmanship-trained, armed citizenry as an American tradition and civic duty essential to national defense (the citizen-soldier or 'prepared citizenry' ideal, including support for the National Board for the Promotion of Rifle Practice framed in patriotic terms); (d) contrasts American gun rights with European, Soviet/Communist, Fascist, Gestapo, or police-state disarmament and tyranny; or (e) urges voting, donations, or activism framed explicitly as defending Second Amendment freedom and American rights. The Americanist framing must be integral to the argument, and firearms must be an actual subject of the text, not merely a metaphor.

positive_examples.text: "A man loves a good gun, for it makes him feel independent and prepared for peace or war." So said Davy Crockett when, more than 125 years ago, the citizens of Philadelphia presented him with "Old Betsy" - the rifle he carried with him to the West and to the glory of the Alamo. So said Fess Parker when he, in turn, presented a replica of "Old Betsy" to Deputy Secretary Robert B. Anderson at NRA's Annual Banquet on April first of this year. So, in truth, has said every one who has belonged to the National Rifle Association of America since its birth more than 84 years ago, for no words can better express the objects of our Association or the convictions of its members. The affinity of a man - or of a boy - for a gun dates back to the early days of antiquity. It started when our earliest ancestor found that a club was of help to him in his struggle for food and existence. If it were a stout stick with straight grain, if it fitted his hand well, and if it had nubs that were efficient, then indeed it was a good club and he learned to love it. It was his constant companion. Sleeping or waking, at home or afield, it was never from his side, an invaluable companion in his search for something to cat or in the defense of his family. As man became wiser, the club was replaced by the hatchet, the hatchet by the bow, the bow by the harquebus, the harquebus by the rifle. Whatever the type of weapon, it has been a true friend of the man who recognized its worth and who knew how to rise it. It was the weapon which gave man a sense of freedom and independence. It was a badge of authority and, many years ago, was limited to the ruling class. As firearms increased in quantity so that even the common man might acquire them, the monarch became less powerful and tyranny lost some of its sting. It was the weapon in the hands of the common people rather than an enlightened government that brought the Magna Charta and the beginning of democracy. When our forefathers came to the shores of North America they were searching for greater freedom than had been their lot in Europe. Like their ancestors before them, they, too, came armed with the weapons of their day. In conquering the wilderness, in their search for game, in defending their cabins against the savage marauder, the blunderbuss, the musket, and the long-rifle all played an important part. They played their part, too, in winning the freedom which the Pilgrims had hoped to find in this new land. The attempt of the British to confiscate their weapons and to disarm the populace was long remembered and long feared. It was that memory and that fear which fostered the adoption of the Second Amendment to the Constitution, guaranteeing the right of the people to keep and to bear arms as necessary to the security of a free state. Unfortunately, the memory and the fear have been dimmed by the years, so that today only the National Rifle Association of America is alert to the danger, and wages a continuous fight for the right of loyal citizens to keep and bear arms for lawful purposes. Food and a gun were synonymous in Davy Crockett's day. Now, however, shooting for fun has taken the place of shooting for sustenance. Those of us who know, find it replete with enjoyment, suited to man or woman, boy or girl. Hunting afield or trying for perfect scores on the target range, the sport of shooting thrives on man's inherent love for a gun. More than any other sport, shooting is not confined to recreation alone. It relates directly to the welfare of the nation. The experience gained while hunting paid dividends at Concord and at Lexington. The victory at New Orleans reflected the peaceful pursuit of game in the backwoods of Tennessee. The stemming of the tide at Chateau-Thierry was the result of innumerable days of training on the target range and of "shooting for fun". It is not sufficient just to like a gun. A man must know how to use it properly, safely, and with accuracy. The education of our youth in safe gun handling, the organization and conducting of a competitive program on a National and International scale, and the training of our able-bodied citizens in marksmanship are major tasks of NRA. We are the leader in these fields of endeavor. We believe in the principles set forth in the Declaration of Independence and in the Constitution of the United States of America. We believe that our independence was achieved because the stout-hearted patriot who battled for it, owned and knew how to use the flintlock of his day. We believe that the safe-guarding of that independence rests in an equally well-armed citizenry, trained in marksmanship. We believe that the right of loyal, law-abiding citizens to purchase, to own, and to use firearms for lawful purposes should not be abridged. We believe that shooting for fun should be encouraged in peace so that we may be better prepared to defend the security of this nation if need be. These are and always have been the basic tenets of the National Rifle Association of America. Davy Crockett's America was a nation of marksmen. The America of our day must become once more a nation of marksmen if we are indeed to feel "independent, and prepared for peace or war".
positive_examples.explanation: The archetypal case: from Davy Crockett's 'Old Betsy' through the Revolution and the Second Amendment to a call that America 'become once more a nation of marksmen' - firearms are woven into founding heritage, freedom, and national identity.

positive_examples.text: Marksmanship training for all American citizens who would be subject to service in the event of war is a valuable contribution to national defense. To prepare ourselves for the variety of military engagements in which we might become involved, we are obliged to maintain a corresponding variety of capabilities within our defense establishment. We must have a stable and continuing defense program because we cannot rely on 'crash programs' in the future. We require the capability to meet any challenge promptly, vigorously, and effectively. National defense is an immediate requirement. What we do today vitally affects our success in any future emergency. In any type of military operations, one thing that has not changed is the importance of the soldier's mastery of his individual weapons, fundamentally the rifle. In fact, this importance has increased. One of the basic requirements of modern warfare is the greatly increased dispersion of units. In order to minimize the effectiveness of an enemy's firepower, our units will be dispersed over a much larger area than ever before. As a result, they will have to be more completely self-sustained and their members will be called upon to exercise an even higher degree of individual self-reliance. Cannoneers, cooks, and clerks must be ready and able to defend themselves against sudden enemy raids. As for the infantryman himself, the rifle is still his basic weapon. We must not forget that the military purpose of war is to achieve control over land and the people who live on it. The ultimate measure of the control which has been attained is the area dominated by the infantryman with the fire of his individual weapon. In the final analysis, the success with which that domination is established, maintained, and extended depends in large part on the soldier's mastery of his rifle. The marksmanship programs conducted by the National Board for the Promotion of Rifle Practice and the National Rifle Association of America for military personnel and civilians are important to our national defense. Qualification firing is excellent training for military and civilians alike. Formal competition plays an important part in encouraging the development of marksmanship. The Small Arms Firing Schools and the National Rifle and Pistol Matches conducted each year at Camp Perry help to maintain the American tradition of a prepared citizenry, trained to do a soldier's job with a soldier's skill when necessity calls. Because of my responsibilities in the Department of Defense and because of my personal lifetime interest in fine marksmanship, I commend those individuals and organizations that promote marksmanship training in time of peace as a vital contribution to preparedness in case of war. I urge continued efforts by our leaders in the Armed Forces and in civilian life to develop better training methods, to improve equipment, and to encourage greater participation in this important activity.
positive_examples.explanation: Illustrates the citizen-soldier/prepared-citizenry strand: civilian and military marksmanship programs 'help to maintain the American tradition of a prepared citizenry, trained to do a soldier's job with a soldier's skill.'

positive_examples.text: The pattern of Communist action is now well established: Limit membership to a few well-disciplined zealots. Talk to and about "the masses" but keep them just outside The Party. Place key men in government departments controlling foreign affairs, national defense, and law enforcement. Get them into labor unions controlling transport, utilities, newspapers and radio, government employees - particularly police. Take it easy. Never expose the iron fist under the silken glove until the time has come to strike. In Hungary before the silken glove was removed, all shooting clubs were closed by legal decree. All privately-owned small arms were taken into "safekeeping" by the police. In Czechoslovakia all patriotic citizens had been disarmed when the arms registration lists were seized by Hitler's Fifth Column. In both countries Communists infiltrated the army and the police departments. When the iron fist struck, loyal troops and police were either disarmed or held in barracks where they could not interfere with the Communist-controlled troops and police. Although all civilians had presumably been disarmed, thousands of armed civilian "auxiliary police" appeared magically on the streets-wearing Party armbands! A "peaceful" revolution is really quite simple. A month ago a State Department official told a committee of Congress that 136 State Department employees had been dismissed during 1947 as a result of loyalty investigations. J. Edgar Hoover, Director of the FBI, had previously told the committee that in checking 401,211 fingerprints of Federal Government employees, 8.5 percent had turned up with criminal records. State and municipal government employees would probably check out with a similar average record. People with a criminal tendency are people quite likely to become useful tools for foreign agents or subversive groups. How can anyone, squarely facing the contemporary record, seek or support laws which would require American citizens to register their privately owned firearms with any municipal, state, or federal agency? Granting that most governmental employees are honest, loyal Americans, we must also grant that only honest, loyal Americans will register their weapons. Certainly the crook and subversive agent will not do so. Who will guarantee that the registration lists of arms owned by reputable, loyal Americans will not, now or in the future, fall into the hands of disreputable, disloyal persons? We have seen in America and in Europe the potent possibilities of unholy alliances between crooks and disloyal persons, inside and outside the Government service. Americans have long worried about the military state. They generally fail to realize that it was the police state which set Mussolini and Hitler into power as it is the police state which now gives the Comintern its strangle-hold on Communist-controlled peoples. As more and more prosecutors step into legislative and executive chairs or move from Bar to Bench, it becomes increasingly important to guard against a dangerous police state psychology unwittingly taking root in American statute books. General firearms registration fits perfectly into the established pattern of Communist action and is at the same time the typical example of police state psychology.
positive_examples.explanation: Illustrates the anti-tyranny contrast strand: Communist takeovers in Hungary and Czechoslovakia began with closing shooting clubs and seizing registration lists, so American firearms registration is framed as a police-state tool.

negative_clarification: Do NOT classify as 1 when: (a) the editorial is patriotic or American-themed but never substantively discusses firearms (e.g., Washington/Lincoln birthdays, Independence Day ideals, democracy essays, war mobilization, universal service, campaign-finance/free-speech fights); (b) the editorial concerns firearms but lacks Americanist framing - safety education and accident prevention, youth/junior programs, technical or military-training critiques, firearm history or artifact stories, industry and business matters, tournament life and sportsmanship, internal NRA governance and membership news, polling or media-bias critiques, and crime-policy pieces that argue enforcement rather than rights; (c) the editorial analyzes gun regulation while accepting or endorsing it, invoking rights only as a passing caution; (d) Americanist language appears only in a single incidental phrase (e.g., 'American in concept,' 'un-American atmosphere') within an otherwise empirical or technical discussion; or (e) shooting is used only as an extended metaphor for politics or citizenship.

negative_examples.text: It is mostly thoughtlessness, it is partly a deliberate effort to create dissension, but whatever the cause there are many Americans who seem to be currently more interested in the fact that they are political officeholders, or bankers, or 'workers' (who isn't?), or merchants, or farmers, than they are interested in the fact that they are first and foremost Americans. February is a good month to remember what it means to be an American. Within the short span of ten days we celebrate, this month, the birthdays of the two men who, more than any others, symbolize for Americans the things which are America. The birthday of Washington, landed aristocrat who risked personal fortune, reputation, life itself, to lead a quarreling, badly organized lot of backwoodsmen, farmers, middle-class merchants, and country gentlemen to moral victory over their own disunity, to military victory over the world's greatest military power, and to the formation of that republic which relighted the beacon of freedom for men all over the world. The birthday of Lincoln, impoverished son of the frontier, who availed himself of the opportunities afforded by that republic to even its lowliest sons and rose to the highest elective office in the gift of his fellow citizens - leading them then through that bloody struggle which preserved the Union and the freedom of the individual that Washington had risked so much to establish. It is fortunate coincidence that, so early in each year, Americans are reminded of the lives of these two men - so superficially different, so fundamentally alike. One to the manor born; the other an orphaned wanderer from cabin to cottage. One carefully garbed in the height of fashion; the other careless of garb in work-a-day clothes. One meticulous in his books of account, canny in his bargaining; the other most interested in the books of the sages, prone to bargain poorly. Each, in his own way, prideful of accomplishment, fine in resolve, a purposeful gambler. Together typifying the whole broad range of qualities, of opportunities, of accomplishments which have made America great. This year, may February 12 and February 22 mean more to us than just some more holidays. May they be days for a hit of personal soul-searching. As we celebrate these birthdays may we quietly, without smugness, without bigotry, resolve to take renewed pride in the simple fact that we are Americans - sole heirs to the traditions, the opportunities, the responsibilities symbolized by George Washington, landed gentleman, and Abraham Lincoln, orphan of the frontier.
negative_examples.explanation: A purely patriotic meditation on Washington, Lincoln, and what it means to be American that never mentions firearms; shows that Americanism alone, without guns, is insufficient.

negative_examples.text: School's out - and so are several million active youngsters. In city, suburb, and country, they are looking for something to do, anything to do which will keep their keen minds and busy feet and fingers on the move. Wise mothers have the arnica bottle and the medicated adhesive tape ready for frequent use, for the season of cut and mashed fingers, sprained ankles, and numerous other minor casualties has arrived. Sadly, too, the hospitals will get their share of major-accident cases. Streets full of playing youngsters will give up their toll from automobiles; unsupervised water sports will exact a penalty; and the back-yard variations of everything from baseball to "duck on a rock" will produce the annual crop of lacerations, sprains, and broken bones. Few of these accidents will attract enough attention to make the newspapers, but there will be other accidents no more serious which will receive black headlines! Boys - and girls - will be accidentally shot as the result of unsupervised use of air rifles and firearms in the hands of untrained playmates. The newspapers will report that many of these accidents occurred at "target practice," but investigation will disclose that the "target practice" consisted of shooting at tin cans, bottles floating down a creek, or some improvised target tacked on a back fence or on the trunk of a green tree. Parents do not try to stop their children from playing baseball because some lad breaks his leg, or suffers a fractured skull from a wildly tossed bat, but in every community hundreds of parents do try to stop their children from handling firearms every time the newspapers report a gun accident! Perhaps the greatest stumbling block to the continued growth, the greatest threat to the very existence, of target shooting as a sport in America is the annual crop of accidents and near-accidents with air rifles and .22-caliber rifles during the vacation period. Consequently every shooting club, every individual shooter, has an immediate personal stake in the problem of eliminating these firearm accidents among the youngsters. That proper training and supervision will eliminate such accidents has been proven by the results attained by The National Rifle Association through its Junior rifle program. More than 68,000 Junior qualification awards were made by The National Rifle Association last year, and more than 145,000 boys and girls received more or less instruction in the handling of .22-caliber rifles, on a thousand Junior ranges throughout the country. Not one youngster received as much as a scratch. No boy or girl who has received rifle instruction under the banner of The National Rifle Association during the twelve years from 1926 to the present, has, to our knowledge, ever been involved in a gun accident. This remains true even though many of them have for several years occupied the state of full maturity, and have taken their places in the hunting fields as well as on senior target ranges. Educators have come to such a complete realization of this fact that this summer fully fifty per cent of those privately conducted camps which by reason of age groups and camp facilities might be expected to include rifle ranges as a part of their equipment, will have such ranges. The National Director of Safety of the Boy Scouts of America has for several years actively recommended the institution of rifle-instruction courses in all Boy Scout Camps where ranges can be safely built. But only a small proportion of our boys and girls attend summer camps. What can be done to provide the same kind of instruction for the rest of our youngsters? There are 60,000 adult members of the N.R.A. Perhaps 40,000 of them are members of the 2,000 Senior Rifle Clubs, and the other 20,000 do not belong to any clubs. If each of the 2,000 Rifle Clubs will set aside Saturday morning or one or two of the long evenings during several weeks of the Summer to teach the youngsters of their community how to handle a rifle safely, they will find the newspapers, the local Safety Council, and other agencies eager and willing to cooperate. The number of gun accidents during the vacation period can most certainly be materially reduced, if not eliminated, and if each of the 20,000 individuals who belong to no club will undertake to instruct the child or children of some friend, an immeasurable volume of good will and of good work will be accomplished. No matter if the senior has to forego a little shooting on his own account; no matter if the club has to postpone the firing of some club match, the elimination of only one gun accident among the youngsters of your community will certainly be more than ample compensation for any sacrifice made. And, strangely enough, once you have undertaken the program you will find that no real sacrifice is involved. Many a man has found that he actually derived keener pleasure from the development of a youngster into a good shot than he ever had from winning a medal for himself! School's out! When the kids troop back to their classrooms in the Fall, will you be able to say: "I did my bit to keep somebody's youngster from getting into trouble with a gun this summer"?
negative_examples.explanation: A firearms piece about preventing summer gun accidents among children through NRA safety training; shows that guns alone, without Americanist framing of rights, liberty, heritage, or national defense, are insufficient.

negative_examples.text: The national political campaign is on its way. The nation is engaged, meanwhile, in a bitter struggle for survival. It is the hope of every real American that the bitterness of the fight will be directed exclusively at the military battle and that the political battle will be confined to coolly logical discussion of the questions properly pertaining to the campaign. The rifleman on the firing line selects his target, casts his "weather eye" aloft to gauge the wind, squints through his glass to determine the trickiness of his mirage, sets his sights, settles into position, holds, and squeezes. He knows in advance that the wind and mirage will be there to throw him off the target. He knows there will be the distracting noises and traffic of a busy range. But he also knows that if he sets his sights properly, concentrates on his own target, disregards the noise and HOLDS and SQUEEZES he will hit what he is shooting at. If he conducts himself like a real sportsman he will be equally popular in victory or defeat. Rarely in the history of our Nation has it been so vital for American men and women to apply the doctrine of the range to their political activities. What is our target? To win the war, of course. But that is in the hands of our military and naval people who have demonstrated their competence and who should keep out of politics, just as politics should keep away from them. Our target as voting citizens of the United States is to preserve our democratic processes and to insure the efficient conduct of our Government. To do those things, we must intelligently seek the facts concerning every debatable question - all the facts, not the facts we like to hear because they come from someone on our side of the political fence. We must, in other words, get up on the firing line, find our target and obtain all the dope we can get that will help us set our sights properly. We may prefer to have someone tell us there is no wind and no mirage, but that information won't get us on the target if in fact, there is a ten mile wind from nine o'clock, or a boiling mirage! The rifleman who insulates himself against information - all he can get, good and bad, from team mates or members of other teams - is no help to his team. The voter who insulates himself from all the information he can get - good and bad, from political friend and political foe - is of no help to his nation! Now as to that second phase of the rifleman's doctrine on the range: that matter of SPORTSMANSHIP. It is possible to conduct a political campaign like sportsmen. It has been done often in the past. Faced with so controversial and involved an issue as the slavery question, Lincoln and Douglas conducted a campaign in which both spoke and acted like gentlemen - to the great benefit of their listeners and the Nation. Most truly successful "big time" political figures are gentlemen and sportsmen in both their personal and political affairs. It is among the smaller fry and the hangers-on, the political opportunists seeking special privileges for themselves and the groups they claim to represent, that decency and good sportsmanship are cast to the winds when the political campaigning begins. Lies, half-truths, innuendo, bigotry, appeals to class against class, are the stock in trade of this group. Calm, logical discussion of fundamental issues: clean, hard punching above the belt, is no part of their stock in trade. Their appeal is to passion and prejudice. They are the kind who would send you to the firing line with a half point left windage when the true dope called for a point and a half. They would start a rumpus behind the firing line when you were half-way through your string in the hope of distracting your attention from the real dope and your own target. For the sake of those who have died to preserve the ideals that are America: for the sake of those yet to die; for the sake of yourself and your children: for the sake of the Nation, be a sportsman in this political campaign, demand sportsmanship of the campaigners; do not be misled or confused by the rabble-rousers. the name-callers, the liars. Your ballot is a bullet fired in the battle for American constitutional government. Get all the dope before you set your sights. Then go into the match and come out of it a SPORTSMAN. . . . Easy does it! Hold and squeeze! . . . Beware the wind and mirage!
negative_examples.explanation: Uses marksmanship as an extended metaphor for conducting a political campaign ('your ballot is a bullet'); shows that figurative references to shooting in a politics piece do not count as being about guns.
